stem: The three major schools of sculpture that developed in the post-Mauryan period were Gandhara, Mathura and __________.
solution: The three main sculptural schools were Gandhara, Mathura and Amaravati.

stem: The Gandhara school of art shows a strong influence of __________ art.
solution: The Gandhara school shows marked Greco-Roman (Hellenistic) influence.

stem: The Gandhara school of sculpture flourished mainly in the region of present-day __________.
solution: Gandhara art developed in the north-west (present Pakistan–Afghanistan region).

stem: The Mathura school of sculpture used __________ stone.
solution: The Mathura school characteristically used red spotted sandstone.

stem: The Gandhara school typically used __________ for its sculptures.
solution: Gandhara sculptures were made of grey-blue schist and later stucco.

stem: The Amaravati school of sculpture flourished on the banks of the __________ river.
solution: The Amaravati school developed in the Krishna river valley of Andhra Pradesh.

stem: The Amaravati school used __________ marble for its sculptures.
solution: The Amaravati school used a distinctive white to greenish-white marble.

stem: The first images of the Buddha in human form are believed to have been made by the __________ schools.
solution: The earliest anthropomorphic Buddha images were made in Gandhara and Mathura.

stem: Before the Buddha was shown in human form, he was represented by __________.
options: symbols like the wheel, footprints and bodhi tree
solution: The early aniconic tradition used symbols such as the wheel, footprints, empty throne and bodhi tree.

stem: The Gandhara Buddha is characterised by __________.
options: wavy hair, sharp features and heavy drapery
solution: Gandhara Buddhas have wavy hair, Greco-Roman features and thick, realistic drapery.

stem: The Mathura Buddha is characterised by __________.
options: a shaven head or snail-shell curls, a delighted expression and light drapery
solution: The Mathura Buddha shows an energetic, delighted face and thin, clinging drapery in Indian style.

stem: The stupa at __________ is famous for its beautifully carved railings (vedika) with narrative relief medallions.
solution: The Bharhut stupa is known for its carved railings with Jataka relief medallions.

stem: The elaborately carved gateways of the Great Stupa at Sanchi are called __________.
solution: The four carved gateways of the Sanchi stupa are called toranas.

stem: The carvings on the Sanchi toranas mainly depict scenes from the __________.
options: Jataka tales and life of the Buddha
solution: The Sanchi gateways depict Jataka stories and events from the Buddha's life.

stem: The chaitya caves at Bhaja, Karle and Kondane belong to the __________ tradition.
solution: These are rock-cut Buddhist chaitya (prayer hall) caves of the post-Mauryan period.

stem: The grandest and best-preserved rock-cut chaitya hall of the period is at __________.
solution: The chaitya hall at Karle is the largest and finest of the early rock-cut chaityas.

stem: A chaitya hall typically ends in an __________ where the stupa is placed.
solution: Chaitya halls have an apsidal (semicircular) rear housing the votive stupa.

stem: The large arched window on the façade of a chaitya cave is called a __________ window.
solution: The horseshoe-shaped opening is the chaitya window (chaitya-arch).

stem: The Kushana ruler who was a great patron of Buddhist art was __________.
solution: The Kushana emperor Kanishka was a great patron of Buddhist art.

stem: The Mathura school also produced images of __________ deities besides the Buddha.
solution: Mathura produced Jain Tirthankaras and Brahmanical (Hindu) deities as well as Buddhas.

stem: The dynasties associated with the post-Mauryan sculptural developments include the Sungas, Satavahanas and __________.
solution: The Sungas, Satavahanas and Kushanas patronised the post-Mauryan art.

stem: The Amaravati stupa reliefs are noted for their __________.
options: dynamic, crowded compositions full of movement
solution: Amaravati reliefs are known for lively, crowded, movement-filled compositions.

stem: The bracket figures of Yakshis on the Sanchi torana are shown in a __________ pose.
solution: The Sanchi bracket Yakshis are salabhanjika figures grasping a tree branch.

stem: The Gandhara school is sometimes called the __________ school of Indian art.
solution: Gandhara art is often called Greco-Buddhist or Indo-Greek art.

stem: The ushnisha (cranial bump) and urna (mark between the brows) on the Buddha image are __________.
options: auspicious marks of a great being
solution: The ushnisha and urna are among the auspicious bodily marks (lakshanas) of the Buddha.

stem: The narrative art on early stupas served mainly to __________.
options: teach the Buddha's life and Jatakas to devotees
solution: The relief carvings narrated the Buddha's life and Jataka stories for devotees.

stem: The dome of a stupa is called the __________.
solution: The hemispherical dome of a stupa is called the anda.

stem: The railing on top of the stupa dome enclosing a small square is the __________.
solution: The harmika is the railed square platform at the top of the dome.

stem: The mast rising from the harmika, bearing umbrellas (chhatra), is called the __________.
solution: The yashti is the central mast bearing the chhatras (umbrellas).

stem: The path for circumambulation (pradakshina) around a stupa is defined by the __________.
solution: The vedika (railing) marks the circumambulatory path around the stupa.

stem: The Satavahana rulers were important patrons of the __________ stupa and school.
solution: The Satavahanas patronised the Amaravati stupa and the Amaravati school.

stem: The 'standing Buddha' from Mathura wears drapery that is __________.
options: thin and clinging, revealing the body
thick and heavy like a toga
solution: The Mathura Buddha wears thin, clinging drapery revealing the body form.

stem: The Buddha image in Gandhara art is often shown with a __________ halo behind the head.
solution: Gandhara Buddhas usually have a plain circular halo behind the head.

stem: The chaitya caves are examples of __________ architecture.
solution: Chaitya halls are rock-cut, excavated into hillsides.

stem: The interior pillars of the Karle chaitya are topped with carved __________.
solution: The Karle chaitya pillars have bell capitals topped with elephant-and-rider figures.

stem: The art of Bharhut is stylistically __________ and shows figures in low relief.
solution: Bharhut sculpture is early in style, with figures carved in flatter, low relief.

stem: The narrative panels at Sanchi and Bharhut mainly illustrate __________.
solution: The panels illustrate Jataka tales and the Buddha's life.

stem: The moustached, muscular Buddha with sharp facial features is characteristic of the __________ school.
solution: The realistic, Greco-Roman-featured Buddha is characteristic of the Gandhara school.

stem: The jovial, fleshy Buddha carved in red sandstone is characteristic of the __________ school.
solution: The energetic, fleshy red-sandstone Buddha is typical of the Mathura school.

stem: The main subject of the Amaravati reliefs was the __________.
options: life of the Buddha and Jatakas
solution: Amaravati reliefs mostly depict the Buddha's life and Jataka stories.

stem: The post-Mauryan period saw the beginning of __________ worship in Indian art.
solution: This period marks the beginning of Buddha-image (iconic) worship.

stem: The 'mithuna' figures carved on early Buddhist monuments represent __________.
solution: Mithuna (loving couple) figures were auspicious motifs on early monuments.

stem: The gateways of the Sanchi stupa face the __________ directions.
solution: The four toranas of Sanchi face the four cardinal directions.

stem: The typical drapery folds of Gandhara Buddha images resemble those of __________ statues.
solution: The heavy, realistic drapery folds resemble Roman statuary.

stem: Which school of art is most associated with the region of Andhra Pradesh?
solution: The Amaravati school flourished in the Krishna valley of Andhra Pradesh.

stem: The Kushana period royal portrait statue of Kanishka (headless) was found at __________.
solution: The famous headless statue of Kanishka was found at Mathura.

stem: Post-Mauryan Buddhist architecture is best studied through its __________.
solution: Stupas, chaityas and viharas are the key architectural forms of this period.

stem: The reliefs of this period are important because they record __________ of ancient India.
solution: The reliefs are valuable records of ancient Indian daily life, dress and society.

stem: The two schools that developed the Buddha image almost simultaneously but in different styles were __________.
solution: Gandhara and Mathura independently developed the Buddha image in distinct styles.

stem: The lasting significance of post-Mauryan art is that it established the __________ of Indian sculpture.
solution: This period established the iconographic and narrative traditions of Indian sculpture.
